The AFRL in-house study assumed a 100 kW solar array.
The AFRL in-house study recommended a combination of the Busek BHT-200 Hall thruster and the AFRL μPPT for a near-term mission.
The Virginia Tech University design study looked at a 50 kW solar array.
The Virginia Tech University study chose to employ pulsed plasma thrusters to meet their propulsion needs.
The Aerophysics, Inc. study developed a dynamic optimization code to analyze alternatives for propulsion on a 500 kW solar array.
The Aerophysics, Inc. study determined that the optimal propulsion system for a 500 kW solar array was a set of notional low power ion engines.
The four PowerSail configurations considered in the Virginia Tech University study were the kite tail, sphere, fan, and flat array.
The key factors in the Virginia Tech University propulsion system optimization were minimizing complexity and integration issues rather than system mass.
The main propulsion options considered in the Virginia Tech University study were ion thrusters, pulsed plasma thrusters, magnetoplasmadynamic thrusters, resistojets, and arcjets.
The main materials considered for the structures subsystem in the Virginia Tech University study were aluminum, steel, magnesium, titanium, beryllium, and composite materials.
The key attitude determination and control sensors considered in the Virginia Tech University study were horizon sensors, rate gyros, sun sensors, GPS receivers, star trackers, and magnetometers.
The key control actuators considered in the Virginia Tech University study were reaction wheels, momentum wheels, control moment gyros, and magnetic torquers.
The Virginia Tech University study provided a more comprehensive look at the entire spacecraft system compared to the AFRL in-house study.
